title: Obtain cultures without an avoidable antibiotic delay
stem: A stable client with an indwelling urinary catheter has orders for a urine culture and a first antibiotic dose. The sampling port is readily accessible and collection can occur now. What is appropriate?
options: Collect the specimen promptly before the first dose
Give the dose and collect urine after symptoms improve
Wait for the culture result before giving the ordered antibiotic
Collect the sample from a previously filled drainage bag
why: Antibiotic exposure can reduce culture yield when sampling is easily obtained first.
Treatment may reduce the chance of identifying the organism.
Specimen collection does not require delaying treatment until results return.
Old bag urine may not reliably represent a fresh diagnostic specimen.
takeaway: Antibiotic exposure can reduce culture yield when sampling is easily obtained first.
learningObjective: Collect an available ordered culture before antibiotics without awaiting the result.

title: Reassess therapy when susceptibility results arrive
stem: A client improving on an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic has a culture identifying a susceptible organism. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Add the targeted medicine while completing the broad-spectrum course
Team review for the most targeted effective regimen
Complete the broad-spectrum course solely because the response is good
Repeat the culture before considering any regimen review
why: Unnecessary overlap adds exposure without automatically improving treatment.
The identified organism and susceptibilities can support narrower effective coverage.
Improvement does not remove the benefit of reviewing unnecessary broad coverage.
Existing clinically relevant susceptibility results can already inform the treatment review.
takeaway: The identified organism and susceptibilities can support narrower effective coverage.
learningObjective: Anticipate targeted antimicrobial review after organism susceptibility becomes available.

title: Clarify an incomplete allergy history
stem: A client reports 'a penicillin allergy' before receiving a newly prescribed antibiotic. No reaction details are recorded. What is the best next step?
options: Remove the allergy because no written proof is available
Request an antibiotic from a different class because penicillins and cephalosporins are both beta-lactams
Ask what happened, when it occurred and what treatment was needed
Assume nausea and airway swelling carry the same risk
why: An undocumented history still needs investigation before removal.
A shared broad class does not establish identical allergy risk for every product; the reaction history and proposed antibiotic need assessment.
Reaction characteristics help the team assess the allergy and antibiotic plan.
Different reaction types require different clinical interpretation.
takeaway: Reaction characteristics help the team assess the allergy and antibiotic plan.
learningObjective: Elicit reaction details before interpreting a nonspecific antibiotic allergy history.

title: Respond to severe antibiotic-associated diarrhea
stem: A client taking antibiotics has six watery stools in eighteen hours, abdominal cramping and increasing thirst. What is most appropriate?
options: Recommend loperamide before evaluating the cause
Give routine intolerance advice because no fever is reported
Arrange a stool sample for the next clinic day before deciding on further care
Assess hydration and report possible antibiotic-associated infection
why: Antimotility treatment may be inappropriate with suspected infectious colitis.
Absence of fever does not exclude important antibiotic-associated infection or dehydration.
Delaying the decision until a later sample does not address current fluid losses and possible transmissible infection.
Frequent diarrhea and thirst raise concerns about colitis and fluid depletion.
takeaway: Frequent diarrhea and thirst raise concerns about colitis and fluid depletion.
learningObjective: Assess significant antibiotic-associated diarrhea for hydration and infectious complications.

title: Interpret antibiotic response using trends
stem: After antibiotics begin for pneumonia, which findings most clearly support improvement? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature trend and respiratory symptoms improve
Usual activity becomes easier at the same oxygen requirement
One normal temperature while an antipyretic is active
Less coughing accompanied by increasing somnolence
A falling white count with worsening hypotension
why: The infection's clinical manifestations should lessen with effective treatment.
Functional improvement adds meaningful evidence of recovery.
This alone can mask fever without establishing infection control.
Reduced cough with declining alertness may indicate deterioration.
Laboratory improvement does not outweigh new circulatory compromise.
takeaway: The infection's clinical manifestations should lessen with effective treatment.
learningObjective: Judge antimicrobial response using clinical trends rather than isolated laboratory changes.

title: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity
stem: A client receiving gentamicin reports new ringing in the ears and unsteadiness. The next dose is due. What is appropriate?
options: Wait until the antibiotic course is complete to arrange testing
Promptly report the symptoms and clarify the next dose
Give the dose because hearing loss has not been confirmed
Treat dizziness with a sedative before administration
why: Delay may allow potentially irreversible injury to progress.
Aminoglycosides can cause auditory and vestibular toxicity.
Early symptoms warrant review before further potentially harmful exposure.
Sedation can obscure neurological assessment without addressing ototoxicity.
takeaway: Aminoglycosides can cause auditory and vestibular toxicity.
learningObjective: Report new auditory or balance symptoms during aminoglycoside exposure.

title: Review aminoglycoside clearance during renal decline
stem: During gentamicin therapy, urine output falls and creatinine rises. The most recent drug level predates these changes. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the dose because less drug reaches the urine
Compare today’s oral intake with yesterday’s before approving the dose
Request prompt review of current levels and dosing
Use the prior drug level to approve the next several doses
why: Reduced elimination generally raises systemic accumulation concerns.
Intake comparison may inform hydration assessment but cannot establish current gentamicin clearance or safety with rising creatinine and falling urine output.
Reduced clearance can increase exposure after a previously acceptable level.
An earlier level may no longer represent the client's exposure.
takeaway: Reduced clearance can increase exposure after a previously acceptable level.
learningObjective: Reassess aminoglycoside clearance after acute renal deterioration.

title: Assess a vancomycin infusion reaction
stem: During IV vancomycin, a client develops flushing and itching over the neck and chest. Blood pressure and breathing remain stable. What should the nurse do first?
options: Continue unchanged because blood pressure is normal
Label all future glycopeptides as confirmed anaphylactic allergies
Reduce the rate until flushing settles, then restore the prescribed rate
Pause the infusion and assess/report the reaction
why: Stable pressure does not justify ignoring a new infusion reaction.
The current findings do not establish that specific immune mechanism.
Symptom improvement after slowing does not establish a safe restart plan; the reaction first needs assessment and an authorized administration decision.
The pattern may be infusion related, but assessment is needed before a revised plan.
takeaway: The pattern may be infusion related, but assessment is needed before a revised plan.
learningObjective: Pause and assess a stable flushing reaction during vancomycin infusion.

title: Recognize a severe cutaneous drug reaction
stem: After starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a client develops fever, a spreading painful rash and mouth sores. What is appropriate?
options: Urgently escalate and withhold further doses pending review
Give the next dose after an antihistamine reduces the itching
Treat mouth sores as thrush separate from a mild skin eruption
Request a routine dose reduction while continuing the medicine
why: Painful rash with mucosal involvement suggests a potentially severe drug reaction.
Reduced itching does not exclude severe mucocutaneous injury or make further exposure safe.
The combined mucosal and painful skin findings require consideration of a severe drug reaction.
Continuing exposure during a possible severe reaction can worsen harm.
takeaway: Painful rash with mucosal involvement suggests a potentially severe drug reaction.
learningObjective: Recognize mucosal involvement and painful rash as a serious antimicrobial reaction pattern.

title: Respond to tendon pain during fluoroquinolone use
stem: A client taking ciprofloxacin reports new Achilles tendon pain without trauma. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue ciprofloxacin, reduce tendon loading and discuss pain at routine follow-up.
Withhold ciprofloxacin, rest the tendon and contact the prescriber promptly.
Continue ciprofloxacin, use gentle calf stretches and report pain if swelling appears.
Withhold ciprofloxacin, rest for two days and restart the course if pain resolves.
why: Reducing activity does not remove the need to stop further exposure and obtain prompt review of new tendon pain.
New tendon pain requires stopping further exposure and avoiding tendon stress while the treatment plan is promptly reviewed.
Stretching loads a potentially injured tendon, and visible swelling is not required before action is needed.
Symptom improvement does not authorize restarting ciprofloxacin; the prescriber must review the antibiotic plan.
takeaway: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendon injury that needs treatment review.
learningObjective: Respond promptly to new tendon pain during fluoroquinolone treatment.

title: Address tetracycline chelation
stem: A client takes doxycycline together with calcium supplements and an antacid each morning. What instruction is most useful?
options: Separate the antacid but continue calcium with doxycycline
Take them together only when a full meal is eaten
Check the product-specific separation interval with the pharmacist
Take an extra doxycycline tablet with the supplements
why: Both mineral sources can affect absorption and require product-specific review.
A meal does not reliably remove this interaction.
Minerals can bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.
Additional dosing is not a safe solution to impaired absorption.
takeaway: Minerals can bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.
learningObjective: Address reduced tetracycline absorption from concurrent mineral-containing products.

title: Differentiate expected rifampin discoloration from danger
stem: A client taking rifampin reports orange urine but no pain, jaundice or systemic symptoms. What is the best response?
options: Stop the medicine until urine becomes clear
Assume orange urine confirms dehydration
Report it as confirmed urinary bleeding
Explain expected discoloration and review symptoms requiring reporting
why: An expected effect alone does not justify interrupting essential therapy.
The medication itself can account for the colour change.
Orange discoloration without assessment is not proof of hematuria.
Rifampin can discolour body fluids without indicating organ injury.
takeaway: Rifampin can discolour body fluids without indicating organ injury.
learningObjective: Distinguish expected rifampin fluid discoloration from warning symptoms of injury.

title: Report vision changes on ethambutol
stem: A client taking ethambutol says colours look different and reading is newly blurred. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly contact the treatment team before further dosing
Wait for the next routine eye appointment in several months
Recommend stronger reading glasses first
Reassure because the client has no eye pain
why: Ethambutol-associated optic toxicity needs timely assessment.
A new change requires earlier review to limit potential injury.
A prescription change should not precede evaluation of possible drug toxicity.
Optic toxicity can occur without pain.
takeaway: Ethambutol-associated optic toxicity needs timely assessment.
learningObjective: Report new vision and colour-perception changes during ethambutol therapy.

title: Evaluate neuropathic symptoms during isoniazid
stem: A client taking isoniazid reports new tingling in both feet and has not been taking prescribed pyridoxine. What is most appropriate?
options: Try wider footwear and reassess whether tingling improves over the coming week
Assess and report the tingling and missed pyridoxine
Restart pyridoxine and wait until the routine visit to mention symptoms
Provide foot-comfort advice and request an analgesic for the discomfort
why: A mechanical explanation should not postpone review of new bilateral tingling during isoniazid treatment with missed supplementation.
Possible isoniazid-related neuropathy and the supplementation plan require review.
Resuming supplementation does not remove the need to assess newly developed neuropathy.
Symptom management alone does not evaluate possible treatment-related neuropathy or address the missed pyridoxine plan.
takeaway: Possible isoniazid-related neuropathy and the supplementation plan require review.
learningObjective: Link new peripheral tingling and missed pyridoxine to isoniazid-treatment review.

title: Support a complex tuberculosis regimen
stem: A client finds the tuberculosis regimen difficult to manage and is considering taking only the tablet that causes least nausea. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Explore adverse effects and arrange regimen support
Explain why the prescribed combination should not be self-selected
Recommend taking only one medicine until appetite returns
Suggest saving omitted tablets to add after treatment ends
Assume missed doses are resolved once symptoms improve
why: Addressing tolerability and practical barriers supports effective combination treatment.
Unplanned partial treatment can promote failure and resistance.
Selective therapy can undermine the intended regimen.
A delayed self-designed course is not an appropriate treatment plan.
Symptom improvement does not establish completion or cure.
takeaway: Addressing tolerability and practical barriers supports effective combination treatment.
learningObjective: Address tuberculosis treatment barriers without permitting self-selected partial regimens.

title: Explain oral vancomycin for intestinal infection
stem: A client prescribed oral vancomycin for C. difficile asks why an IV route is not automatically stronger. What is the best explanation?
options: IV treatment would be preferred if venous access were easier
The routes can be exchanged at the same dose when necessary
Oral treatment is reserved only for mild intestinal disease
Oral treatment reaches the intestinal infection site
why: Access convenience does not determine vancomycin delivery to the intestinal lumen.
Their distribution and therapeutic roles are not interchangeable.
Route choice for intestinal vancomycin is not simply a marker of mild illness.
The route is chosen for drug delivery to the target site rather than general IV superiority.
takeaway: The route is chosen for drug delivery to the target site rather than general IV superiority.
learningObjective: Explain why the intestinal treatment target determines oral vancomycin's role.

title: Administer oral nystatin for local effect
stem: A client prescribed nystatin oral suspension immediately swallows it without distributing it in the mouth. What teaching is most useful?
options: Follow the prescribed directions for contact with affected oral surfaces
Mix it into a full drink to eliminate the taste
Stop treatment as soon as the first patch disappears
Use it immediately before rinsing vigorously with water
why: Local contact is important when treating oral candidiasis.
Dilution and rapid swallowing may reduce useful oral contact.
Visible improvement does not automatically establish course completion.
Immediate rinsing may remove medicine from the treatment area.
takeaway: Local contact is important when treating oral candidiasis.
learningObjective: Teach oral nystatin contact with affected mucosal surfaces.

title: Review fluconazole with anticoagulation
stem: A client stable on warfarin is newly prescribed fluconazole. What should the nurse ensure?
options: Advise extra vitamin K foods to offset the new drug
Interaction review and an appropriate anticoagulation-monitoring plan
Continue usual monitoring because both doses are standard
Take warfarin and fluconazole at different times of day to prevent the interaction
why: Unplanned dietary compensation makes anticoagulation less predictable.
Fluconazole can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
Standard doses do not exclude a clinically significant interaction.
Timing separation does not prevent the metabolic effect that can increase warfarin exposure.
takeaway: Fluconazole can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
learningObjective: Plan interaction monitoring when fluconazole is added to warfarin.

title: Assess a QT-risk antibiotic combination
stem: A client prescribed azithromycin takes another QT-prolonging medicine and has potassium below the supplied reference range. What is appropriate?
options: Separate the two medicines by one hour
Check pulse regularity and proceed if the pulse remains regular
Clarify the regimen and electrolyte correction/monitoring plan
Give the antibiotic because there is no current chest pain
why: Timing separation does not reliably remove their electrophysiological interaction.
A regular palpable pulse does not measure QT interval or remove hypokalaemia-related dysrhythmia risk.
Combined QT risk and hypokalemia can increase dysrhythmia risk.
Dysrhythmia risk can exist without chest pain.
takeaway: Combined QT risk and hypokalemia can increase dysrhythmia risk.
learningObjective: Integrate electrolyte and medication risks before administering a QT-prolonging antibiotic.

title: Review clarithromycin with a statin
stem: A client taking simvastatin receives a new clarithromycin prescription. While urgently clarifying this interaction, which additional symptom assessment is particularly relevant?
options: Persistent dry cough with throat irritation
Ringing in the ears with loss of balance
Constipation with dry mouth and urinary hesitancy
New muscle pain, weakness or dark urine
why: That pattern is more characteristic of another drug class than this interaction.
This is an important adverse-effect pattern but not the principal simvastatin interaction concern.
These suggest anticholinergic effects rather than the primary muscle-toxicity risk.
Clarithromycin can increase simvastatin exposure and the risk of serious muscle injury.
takeaway: Clarithromycin can increase simvastatin exposure and the risk of serious muscle injury.
learningObjective: Recognize muscle-injury symptoms as the key toxicity concern with clarithromycin and simvastatin.

title: Identify a potassium-raising antibiotic interaction
stem: A client taking ramipril develops new weakness after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Potassium rises from 4.4 to 5.8 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0), while creatinine is unchanged and the radial pulse is regular. What should the nurse do next?
options: Promptly report the potassium trend, weakness and medicines for rhythm and treatment review
Arrange a repeat potassium at tomorrow’s routine blood draw because creatinine is unchanged
Continue the current regimen while checking for an irregular pulse at routine observations
Separate ramipril and the antibiotic between morning and evening doses
why: The drug combination can raise potassium; a new elevation with weakness needs prompt clinical review despite a currently regular pulse.
Stable creatinine does not exclude a medication-related potassium rise or justify postponing assessment of new symptoms.
A regular palpable pulse does not exclude an important potassium disturbance or establish the regimen is safe to continue.
Dose spacing does not remove the potassium-retaining effects of trimethoprim and ACE inhibition.
takeaway: Assess a new symptomatic potassium rise during interacting therapy even when creatinine and pulse appear stable.
learningObjective: Integrate potassium trend, new symptoms and interacting therapy to select prompt treatment review.

title: Clarify antibiotic delivery with continuous feeds
stem: A client receives continuous enteral nutrition and a new antibiotic through the tube. Pharmacy identifies an interaction with the feed's minerals. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the antibiotic amount to compensate for reduced absorption
Obtain a product-specific timing or alternative-route plan
Apply the same two-hour feed hold used for another antibiotic
Mix the antibiotic directly into the feed to dilute minerals
why: Unprescribed dose compensation is unreliable and potentially unsafe.
The interaction and nutrition requirements need coordinated management.
The appropriate interval depends on this product, the interaction and nutrition requirements; a schedule for another antibiotic is not interchangeable.
Mixing may worsen binding and make dosing incomplete.
takeaway: The interaction and nutrition requirements need coordinated management.
learningObjective: Coordinate antibiotic administration with a mineral-containing continuous enteral feed.

title: Reassess presumed lower urinary infection
stem: A client treated with nitrofurantoin for cystitis develops fever, flank pain and vomiting. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue the lower-UTI plan if an antiemetic relieves vomiting
Arrange repeat urine testing at the next routine visit to compare with the initial sample
Promptly assess possible upper infection and review the regimen
Request a urinary analgesic to address the new flank discomfort
why: Reduced vomiting would not remove the significance of fever and flank pain.
Routine delayed sampling is insufficient for newly systemic and flank symptoms that may indicate upper-tract infection.
Fever, flank pain and vomiting suggest progression beyond bladder-focused treatment.
Pain relief alone does not assess a possible upper urinary infection.
takeaway: Fever, flank pain and vomiting suggest progression beyond bladder-focused treatment.
learningObjective: Reassess presumed cystitis when systemic and flank symptoms develop during therapy.

title: Plan antibiotic use after discharge
stem: A client leaves hospital with an antibiotic course and asks what to do if symptoms settle or adverse effects develop. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep remaining doses for a similar illness months later
Share unused doses with someone who has the same symptoms
Restart the entire course independently after a missed dose
Take the medicine for the prescribed course unless the team changes the plan
Report severe adverse effects promptly for treatment advice
why: Future symptoms may have a different cause requiring reassessment.
Similar symptoms do not establish the same infection or prescription.
Missed-dose management does not usually mean an unreviewed new course.
Duration should follow the individualized treatment plan rather than symptom-based guessing.
Serious reactions may require urgent review and an altered regimen.
takeaway: Duration should follow the individualized treatment plan rather than symptom-based guessing.
learningObjective: Teach prescribed antibiotic duration, missed-dose guidance and adverse-effect escalation.

title: Assess home IV antibiotic readiness
stem: A client will manage home IV antibiotic therapy with nursing support. Which demonstrations support safe discharge planning? Select all that apply.
options: The client explains how to report fever, rash or line problems
The client follows the taught aseptic connection procedure
The client plans to change infusion speed whenever running late
The client recognizes the bag by colour but cannot confirm its label
The client expects the pump alarm to identify every site complication
why: Recognizing complications supports timely contact and reassessment.
Observed technique helps establish practical ability to handle the system.
Unprescribed rate changes can cause adverse effects or delivery problems.
Appearance alone does not verify drug, dose or intended client.
Infiltration or inflammation may occur without a reliable pump alarm.
takeaway: Recognizing complications supports timely contact and reassessment.
learningObjective: Evaluate practical readiness for supported home intravenous antibiotic therapy.
